fields.Text: The two pre-relational data models are the {{c1::hierarchical}} model and the {{c2::network}} model.
The most popular hierarchical DBMS is IBM's {{c1::IMS}}, which is still being used.
The hierarchical model is based on {{c1::records}} (grouped into record types) and {{c2::parent-child relationships}}.
A parent-child relationship type is a {{c1::1:M}} relationship between {{c2::two record types}}.

fields.Front: What is an occurrence (instance) of a PCR?
fields.Back: One parent record together with a number of records of the child record type.

fields.Front: What three situations does the hierarchical model have trouble modelling?
fields.Back: M:N relationships; a record type that is a child in more than one PCR type; n-ary relationships with more than two participating types.

fields.Front: What is the rule for mapping an M:N relationship to the hierarchical model?
fields.Back: Only 1:N can be modelled, so represent the M:N relationship as if it were 1:N and use pointers to save on duplication of data.

fields.Front: Where is the data redundancy in the hierarchical company example?
fields.Back: An employee who works on several projects appears as a child record under each project, so the same employee's data is stored multiple times.

fields.Front: Who designed the network model, when, and what is it often called?
fields.Back: The CODASYL committee (Conference on Data System Languages) in 1971; often called the CODASYL model. A popular DBMS: IDMS.

fields.Text: The network model was designed by the {{c1::CODASYL}} committee in {{c2::1971}}; a popular DBMS using it is {{c3::IDMS}}.
The network model's two basic data structures are {{c1::records}} and {{c2::sets}}.

fields.Front: What is a set type in the network model, and what are its three elements?
fields.Back: A 1:N relationship between two record types, consisting of a name for the set, an owner record type and a member record type.

fields.Text: A network-model set type has three elements: a {{c1::name}}, an {{c2::owner record type}} and a {{c3::member record type}}.

fields.Front: How does the network model differ from the hierarchical model regarding parents?
fields.Back: A record type can participate as owner or member in any number of set types, so a record can have several 'parents' (no tree restriction).

fields.Text: Network-model set occurrences are implemented as {{c1::circular linked lists}}.

fields.Front: List the navigation operations the network model supports.
fields.Back: Given an owner, find all members of the set occurrence; given an owner, find the first/nth/last member; given a member, find the next/previous member; given a member, find the owner.

fields.Front: State the four rules for mapping an ER diagram to the network model.
fields.Back: 1. Regular entities -> record type. 2. Weak entities -> record type. 3. 1:1 and 1:N -> a set type (1:1: pick either as owner; 1:N: the one side is the owner). 4. M:N -> create a linking record type X and make it the member in two set types. (The instructor says you do NOT need to know how to map an ER diagram to the network model; know the models and their problems.)

fields.Text: The relational model was introduced by {{c1::Codd}} in {{c2::1970}}; most DBMSs today are based on it.

fields.Front: How does the relational model represent a database?
fields.Back: As a collection of relations; each relation is a table, which is a set of rows, each row being a collection of related data values.

fields.Front: What analogy does the instructor use for the relational model's importance in databases?
fields.Back: It is 'the Meryl Streep of acting or the Beatles of rock and roll': the be-all and end-all of databases, and the rest of the course is dedicated to it.

fields.Front: In the hierarchical company tree, in which three places is the same employee's data stored?
fields.Back: As an employee under the department, as a supervisee under another employee (SSN and name stored twice), and as a worker under each project the employee works on.

fields.Text: The instructor's rule of thumb: 'In a really good model for a database you don't have to store things {{c1::twice}}.'

fields.Front: According to the instructor, what was the hierarchical model good at and where did it need a 'weird pointer'?
fields.Back: It was great with one-to-many relationships; for many-to-many relationships it had to make up pointers to make things work.

fields.Front: What realisation about data and code drove the new database models of the 1970s?
fields.Back: That data should be separated from code: code accesses the data, but changing how data is stored should not break the code, and changing the code should not break the stored data.

fields.Front: What example does the instructor give of a network-model set occurrence?
fields.Back: A course (owner, e.g. Computer Science) with the students registered in it (members), linked in a circular linked list.

fields.Front: Who was Ted Codd and what was his famous 1970 paper called?
fields.Back: A mathematician (formerly a university professor) working at IBM; the paper was 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'.

fields.Front: What three problems does the instructor say Codd's relational model solved?
fields.Back: It got rid of the issue with many-to-many relationships, kept everything connected ('glued together') so queries were possible, and avoided redundancy (repeated data).

fields.Front: When does the relational model fall short, and what do such companies use instead?
fields.Back: For massive data volumes (Google-scale) it is less suitable, so NoSQL databases were developed; most reasonably sized companies still use a relational database as their primary database.

fields.Text: The instructor says you do {{c1::not}} need to know how to map an ER diagram to the {{c2::network}} model; you need to know the two older models and why they struggled.

fields.Front: What personal anecdote does the instructor give about the hierarchical model still being used?
fields.Back: When she was job hunting, newspaper job ads listed experience with this model as a required skill; she believes companies still run software built on it (IBM's IMS).
